title: How big should battles be?
author: Just-Routine967
selftext:
3000v3000 performance test for large set piece battles ☺️ is it too chaotic or do I go higher?

I've always wanted something like the persistent scenarios (Liberation, CTI) from Arma 3 but at a much larger scifi scale, I think it's shaping up well.

Don't have much of value to add in terms of workflow tips, it's just been an Opus overseer coordinating sessions with their own sections to implement. Blender + Godot and one Tripo model (the ally soldier)

comments.author: deject3d
comments.body: is more big more fun? what tradeoffs are being made?

replies.author: Just-Routine967
replies.body:
I think it's fun watching waves of dropships coming in, drop pods streaking down from the flagship, knowing it isn't just random background set dressing but all fully simulated.
But I'm pretty biased as fps/strategy games of this scale are niche so my bar isn't high.

Tradeoffs?

replies.author: deject3d
replies.body: certainly there are some tradeoffs being made in the AI fidelity or design that enables you to accomodate 6000 units

replies.author: Just-Routine967
replies.body:
They don't have much agency beyond their orders currently, similar to most rts units. 
Maybe once I implement a smart order system that gives them more autonomy similar to Steel Division 2 I'll have to make tradeoffs but at the moment the only thing bottlenecking it is the crowd animations still being CPU bound.

comments.author: mrpoopistan
comments.body:
Not this big.  
  
The combat doesn't look especially fun in this form. It just looks like thousands of guys running around. There's no rhyme or reason to what's happening.

I'll also add that introducing any kind of intelligence to the in-game fighters will slow things down dramatically because you have to introduce loops for their intelligent responses to the environment and the combat situation.

There's a reason the most successful shooters tend to be somewhere between squad and platoon level. EA has pretty much always hovered around that level with the Battlefield/Battlefront games, for example.

replies.author: Just-Routine967
replies.body: Fair, do you feel the same way about combat in games like total war? Is it the perspective that makes it feel overwhelming, having no birds eye view to tell at a glance what the situation is?

replies.author: mrpoopistan
replies.body:
Total War doesn't do an especially great job of depicting shooter-level combat, even in the few eras where firearms are prevalent. (IIRC, Empire TW is the only one that's truly gunpowder era.)

Also, there is the core question of what makes something a game. A game's mechanics have to sit in the player's head and be executable. Again, there's a reason most popular franchises don't do gigantic battles. Even TW uses fairly simple individual combatant logic, focusing on unit-level intelligence.

I will reiterate that the intelligence issue is particularly a problem. To have intelligent combatants, you need either extensive polling for each AI combatant or you need human players. Either way, the process of putting that into the game pushes up against the 16ms or so level you want to be at per frame for 60 fps or higher. For thousands of combatants, that becomes cumbersome.

There's nothing here that suggests a birds-eye view, BTW. That's a whole other game.

replies.author: Just-Routine967
replies.body:
I'm interested to see how they'll handle it in Total War 40k, whether they'll have more squad level tactics stuff going on.

How intelligent do they need to be? If I go too far with autonomy it could seem like they are unresponsive. Each squad already bounds in two fireteams and array themselves to cover multiple sightlines.

I like the idea of having macro/smart orders similar to Steel Division where I can select a whole company, designate them a town to hold and they'll dig in/garrison appropriately. 

The campaign enemy already builds fieldworks like trenches, barbed wire lines and gun emplacements along contested fronts, I could likely recycle that.

replies.author: mrpoopistan
replies.body:
Intelligence in this case means how much individual combatants are polling what's around them. Obv, you'd love for them to be as intelligent as possible. However, polling introduces milliseconds of computations. That eventually leads to frame pacing issues or straightup FPS issues because you have to sync the behavior to what's on screen.

There are ways to economize, such as pre-training (this is how the Forza series does it with AI racers, for example). You can also probably spread some of the logic out over the formation (which is what TW does). Flow dynamics work if you don't especially care about the combatants' individual behavior.

Ultimately, the question is whether the horde you're producing pays off in gameplay. Does it need to be a horde? EA, for example, has found that players aren't especially fond of gigantic numbers of opponents in Battlefield.

If there's an argument for the horde as an enjoyable game mechanic, knock yourself out. But I would definitely test it with players before overcommitting to it.

replies.author: Just-Routine967
replies.body:
Good points. Real campaign battles probably won't go over 1000 units in any one area, and a lot of the time you're commanding from the bridge or mobile FOB where you have a greater idea of what's going on.

Large scale movement for far squads is done through flow fields, only units within 800m have individual pathfinding. I can give a rundown on all the current capabilities/intelligence of the units and the optimizations made to achieve it if you'd like?

Even if I don't use the massive hordes for this I can always reuse the system for other large scale strategy projects so I'm not worried about overcommitting.

replies.author: mrpoopistan
replies.body:
The intelligence issue is largely something to keep an eye on. If you're not seeing pacing issues yet, that's fine.

BTW, Opus (if that's what you're using) does not do good work with frame pacing. It tends to favor a "make it work" strategy. I've had success using Astra as a code auditor to clean up Opie's work. In particular, Opie is no discerning about what should run in the GPU versus the CPU, tending to load more on CPU than it should.

Especially if you want to scale up, that's something you'll want to deal with architecturally now. I keep a markdown in my source code explaining these provisions so the LLMs understand that pacing is important to how it constructs any intelligence within the game.

replies.author: Just-Routine967
replies.body:
I have caught a few instances of that 'just make it work' type mistakes early on which I've so far eliminated. 
All additions are building towards the planned limits while keeping 99% of frames under 16.7ms, not just what will pass the current tests as quickly as possible.
CPU/GPU allocation is the last remaining step for pushing unit count higher in the full detail bubble, crowds are still animated on the main cpu thread 😂. 
The coarser simulations outside the bubble can comfortably run 500k+ units.

replies.author: mrpoopistan
replies.body: Opie very much reminds me of some programmers I know.

comments.author: DaStompa
comments.body:
small suggestion: your projectiles are moving too fast and have no weight, crating a lot of "strobing"effects

you need to figure out a way of giving them meaningful impact, right now you look over and there's obviously an ocean of projectiles flying over everyones heads but it doesn't look like anything

replies.author: Just-Routine967
replies.body: I agree, they look a bit too much like lasers at the moment. Thanks for the feedback

comments.author: Just-Routine967
comments.body: If enough people seem interested I'll clean it up and release a demo/playtest version
